question: How could Abu Lahab be commanded to believe when the Qur'an foretold that he would never believe?
asked: My friend and I were discussing the case of Abu Lahab. How could Allah ask him to believe when a part of that belief was that he cannot believe, because the Qur'an mentions he's going to Jahannam? Is this not a contradiction?
answer:
I can rephrase. Was Abu Lahab required to believe in Islam? If no, how come? If yes, how could he believe when a part of that belief is that he's not going to believe?

> تَبَّتْ يَدَا أَبِي لَهَبٍ وَتَبَّ مَا أَغْنَىٰ عَنْهُ مَالُهُ وَمَا كَسَبَ

Allah revealed the Qur'an. There are only two people from the era of the Prophet ﷺ mentioned by name in the whole Qur'an. We're not talking about Fir'awn and Musa and Ibrahim; in the time of the Prophet ﷺ, there are two individuals mentioned by name in the Qur'an. The first of them is Abu Lahab: "Tabbat yada Abi Lahab." The second of them: "Falamma qada Zaydun minha wataran," Zayd.

So this person is saying: how can Abu Lahab be expected to believe when a part of that belief is that he's not going to believe? And so he's asking: is this not an impossibility or a contradiction?

Now, we begin by stating that sometimes some questions are of detriment to our own iman. They open up a Pandora's box, a discussion and back and forth, qila wa qal, that is of no benefit whatsoever. Not every question is beneficial; not every answer is something that we can grasp and understand. And that is why in the Qur'an Allah says, "Ya ayyuhalladhina amanu la tas'alu 'an ashya'a in tubda lakum tasu'kum": O you who believe, do not ask questions that, if you found out about them or you got deeper into them, might actually cause you doubt and harm.

Some people misunderstand this verse. Allah is never saying don't ask questions about haram and halal. We must know our deen. If you have to do something, it's your job to ask a shaykh, a mufti: is this haram or halal? Allah is saying don't ask questions that are of no value, and when you find out about them, they might actually hurt or harm you.

And the context explains this verse to us, and I'll just briefly go into this tangent. One day the Prophet ﷺ said, "Ask me any question you want. Ask me any question." So one of the new converts, one of the bedouins visiting Madinah, stood up and asked a very foolish question. He said, "Ya Rasulallah, tell me about my father: is he in Jannah or Jahannam?" He had passed away, and the man's father was an idol worshipper. So the Prophet said, "Your father is in Jahannam." So the man became very hurt at this. Then Allah said: why did you ask the question? Why did you ask? It's not useful to you to know. What happened is khalas, it's gone. You are not going to benefit from knowing. So this verse is used when the answer to the question at hand is not going to benefit us at all, and it is possible that this question of Abu Lahab is in this realm also.

There's an interesting hadith of the Prophet ﷺ as well, and that is: my ummah, he said, my ummah will be upon good as long as they don't believe in astrology, the nujum, and as long as they don't ask about the fate of the children of pagans. What's going to happen to the children who died? Will they go to Jannah? Will they go to Jahannam? And this is another common question that we get.

Now, interestingly enough, this question of the children of the non-Muslims, I will actually get there one day inshallah, and I'll tell you, believe it or not, there are ten opinions amongst our ulama. The Prophet ﷺ said don't ask, and our ulama have ten opinions, and we'll go over all of them. But here's the point: why did he say don't ask about the children of pagans? Our scholars say: because the answer is of no practical value to us. What do we gain? How is it going to affect us? So it's as if our Prophet ﷺ is saying: my ummah will be upon good as long as they don't go splitting hairs, as long as they don't go into such issues that are of no value to them. This is perhaps the gist of the hadith.

So with this disclaimer, and perhaps this question of Abu Lahab is amongst them, we will then actually attempt to answer the question. And I will say that you and your friend are not the first people in the ummah to think of this controversy. Maybe you would like to think that, but no. Great ulama and theologians have thought of this from the beginning of time.

This question actually comes under an aspect of theology that is a very, very advanced aspect of theology. It is called the issue of at-taklif bima la yutaq, and that translates as: can Allah obligate on an individual something that the individual is not capable of doing? Taklif means Allah has put a burden; ma la yutaq, that the person has no taqah, no power, to do. And this is a classical controversy, and you have all of the schools of Islam. The Mu'tazila said this is not allowed. Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari and al-Baqillani said this is something that Allah is capable of doing. And others have given their positions.

Ibn Taymiyyah has a very interesting response, and it is the one that I will conclude this question with. Because this is an example that they mention as well: Abu Lahab is being told to believe, and a part of his belief is that he will not believe. Right? Abu Lahab is commanded to believe, and a part of that belief is that he will not believe. It's an oxymoron. So this is the classic example given for at-taklif bima la yutaq.

Ibn Taymiyyah says: putting a burden on somebody that that person cannot do is divided into two categories. The first of them cannot happen, and the second of them can happen.

The first of them is when Allah tells someone to do something that the person is physically incapable of doing. And he said that Allah says in the Qur'an that Allah will never do this, and Allah has never done it. And Ibn Taymiyyah gives the example of saying to a person that he should fly. Allah is saying you should fly: this is impossible, and Allah will not ever put a command of something that is impossible.

> لَا يُكَلِّفُ اللَّهُ نَفْسًا إِلَّا وُسْعَهَا

Another example is somebody who, let's say, has a paralysis or disease; somebody cannot walk, and Allah says you must walk. No, Allah is not going to tell him to do that.

The second category is to require somebody to do something that the person is not capable of doing because the person is doing the opposite at the same time. So for example, to tell the kafir to believe, and the kafir is a kafir, so he's not believing, and Allah knows that the kafir will remain a kafir. But it's not impossible for the kafir to become a believer. Rather, the kafir is being told to do something that the kafir is capable of doing, but he's not going to do it, because he is busy with the opposite of iman, and that is kufr.

So technically it's not impossible in the linguistic sense; it is possible. But it is going to be an impossibility, because that kafir, in the knowledge of Allah, will forever remain a kafir. And so even though Allah is commanding him to accept iman and to be a Muslim, still the person will not do that, in the knowledge of Allah. And so one could say the kafir is being told to do something he will not do, but it is not an impossibility. The kafir can do this.

And this is the response that can be given: yes, in one sense, Abu Lahab was commanded to believe in Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala; in another sense, Allah knew he would never believe.

And so some have argued that this verse is actually a miracle, because if Abu Lahab had publicly proclaimed iman, it would have thrown a spanner in the works. It would have been a big confusion: now what is to be done? And so some have argued this is in fact a mu'jizah from Allah: Allah is telling Abu Lahab that you're going to go to Jahannam, and Abu Lahab is living five years, ten years, and he never challenges this. And this is a valid interpretation as well, or a valid claim to make.

So at the end of the day, we say that Allah will never tell a human to do that which is impossible for the human to do. But Allah 'azza wa jall will burden a person with something the person might choose not to do, and he cannot blame anybody. He cannot blame Allah; he can only blame himself. Abu Lahab refused to accept Islam, and so Allah predicted that he will be in the Nar: "sayasla naran dhata lahab." And that is not a contradiction. It is not something that is putting the impossible on any human being.

So to conclude: **Allah 'azza wa jall will never burden somebody with something that is physically impossible for the person to do.**
